back: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
High mp/bp, conduct when molten/aqueous only, often water-soluble, brittle.
Higher ionic charges and smaller ionic radii.

front: Why do metals form cations and non-metals form anions?
back: Metals have few valence electrons and low IE, so lose them; non-metals have nearly full outer shells, so gain electrons — both reach a noble-gas configuration.

front: Deducing the formula of an ionic compound?
back: Balance charges so the total is zero: Al³⁺ + O²⁻ → Al₂O₃; Ca²⁺ + NO₃⁻ → Ca(NO₃)₂.
-ide: simple anion of one element (chloride Cl⁻, oxide O²⁻). -ate: oxyanion containing oxygen (sulfate SO₄²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻).

front: Structure of an ionic lattice (e.g. NaCl)?
back: Giant 3D lattice of alternating cations and anions; each Na⁺ surrounded by 6 Cl⁻ and vice versa. Formula = simplest ratio, not a molecule.
Enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic solid is separated into its gaseous ions: e.g. NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g); always endothermic (positive).

front: Which has the higher lattice enthalpy, MgO or NaCl? Why?
back: MgO: ions have double the charges (2+/2−) and are smaller, so electrostatic attraction is much stronger.

front: Why doesn’t solid NaCl conduct electricity?
back: Ions are held in fixed lattice positions and cannot move; when molten or aqueous, the ions are mobile. (Electrons do not carry the current.)
A force shifts layers so like-charged ions line up; repulsion splits the crystal.

front: Why do many ionic compounds dissolve in water?
back: Polar water molecules surround the ions (ion–dipole attractions, hydration), releasing energy that compensates for breaking the lattice.

front: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points and low volatility?
back: Many strong, non-directional electrostatic attractions throughout the giant lattice need a lot of energy to overcome.

front: How does electronegativity difference relate to ionic character?
back: Larger ΔEN → more ionic character. Bonding is a continuum; ΔEN > ~1.8 usually treated as predominantly ionic (use the bonding triangle).

front: Why are Roman numerals used in iron(II) chloride?
back: Transition metals form ions with variable charges; the numeral gives the oxidation state: iron(II) = Fe²⁺ → FeCl₂; iron(III) chloride → FeCl₃.

front: Order of radius: Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ (isoelectronic)?
back: Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > Al³⁺: same 10 electrons but increasing nuclear charge pulls them closer.
